_about: The passages Scripture Memory offers as a weekly suggestion. Canonical locations and editorial metadata only — never a word of Scripture. The words are read out of data/bible/ in whichever edition the reader locked when they began, exactly as every other surface in this app resolves a reference.

_authoring.theBar: A reader may choose any eligible passage for themselves from the Bible. This list is different: the app puts these in front of somebody unasked, as THIS WEEK'S VERSE. That is a higher bar. Each one has to stand on its own, mean the same thing alone as it does in its paragraph, and be worth the weeks it will take.
_authoring.whatBelongsHere: Short, coherent alone, and worth carrying. Breadth across the canon matters more than covering a topic, and a verse earns its place by being worth memorising rather than by being recognised.
_authoring.whatDoesNot: A verse that only means what people think it means once it is lifted out. Length is not the only test — a short verse can still be a misquotation when it stands alone, and a promise whose condition is in the next sentence is not a promise.
_authoring.boundaries: Where a range was widened it was widened for a reason recorded in MEMORY-REVIEW.md: a pronoun with no referent inside the selection, a contrast with only one half, or a promise whose qualification sits in the following verse.
_authoring.superscriptions: A psalm whose first verse opens with its own title — the author, the choirmaster, the tune — is not offered here, because the practice would blank words inside a filing label. Nothing is removed from Scripture to make a passage fit; the passage is simply not recommended. See notRecommended below.
_authoring.status: Every entry has been read in its own paragraph and approved. `npm run memory:verify` prints anything still proposed.

notRecommended.why: Addressed to exiles in Babylon about a seventy-year timeline, and the most reliably proof-texted verse in English-speaking Christianity. Alone it teaches close to the opposite of what it says. Jeremiah 29:10-11 would be responsible, but it needs the exile explained, which a weekly card does not do.

In context it is about contentment in plenty and in want. Alone it reads as a promise about performance. Philippians 4:12-13 would be safe and is recorded in MEMORY-REVIEW.md as an open question of catalogue balance rather than of safety.

A proverb is a genre of general truth, not a guarantee. There is no boundary that fixes this, because the issue is genre rather than range, and it is routinely carried as a guarantee by parents who then blame themselves.

Every shipped edition prints the psalm's title inside verse 1 — 'A Psalm by David', 'Salmo de David', '大卫的诗'. A memory drill would hide words inside the title. Held rather than rewritten: Scripture is not edited to fit a feature.
The same, and worse: the choirmaster, the sons of Korah and the tune occupy most of verse 1 before the sentence about refuge begins.
Sound, and a reader may choose it. Held from the weekly rotation only because it says nearly what Isaiah 41:10 already says here, and its commission is tied to one man and one conquest.
